name: Umar Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at your agency look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a four-designer team making public-health leaflets and local festival identities. My master’s in design taught me research, but my useful skill is finding the line people actually misunderstand on a notice board. I use AI every day for early layouts and image variations; I still interview the client and check the public proof.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things outside work at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a small flat alone, earn about the usual designer wage here, and have four months of expenses saved. There are a few agencies within a bus ride, though I would not call that a safety net if they all lose the same clients. I like the team, but I keep a ledger of what each campaign actually pays us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI Plateau resembles the tools already open on my desk. The question for us is still whether a resident can understand a clinic notice when it is pinned above a noisy waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and rent look steady if little changes, and four months saved gives me room to breathe. I would like more time for the awkward public-language checks, but I am not secretly planning to quit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep reviewing clinic leaflets with staff who answer patients' questions, and ask the agency owner to count those review hours in quotes. In the first year of small change, I would put the normal monthly amount into savings and use the existing image tool for first layouts only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own work. I would not call a prettier leaflet a success if patients still arrive on the wrong day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you remember a leaflet you changed after talking to staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vaccination notice used the word registration when the receptionist meant walk-in. I changed the heading after she counted the callers asking for a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need a new AI course in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use the image tool daily already, and a quiet year does not give me a new tool to learn. I would rather pay the receptionist for an hour of testing.

say: I would say **AI drafts** are already part of our ordinary layout work.
I would ask whether **clinic readers** understand the final public notice.
think: I expect my **design work** and rent payments to remain steady.
I have **four months saved** and no plan to leave a useful team.
do: Keep **reviewing clinic leaflets** with reception staff and count that time in agency quotes.
Keep the **usual monthly saving** and use existing image tools only for first layouts.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own wage in a quiet AI year.
S0.quote: I would not call a prettier leaflet a success if patients still arrive on the wrong day.
fieldNote: He defines design quality through **public understanding**, especially receptionist feedback.
Daily use of the **existing image tool** is ordinary agency work, not new AI learning or training.

steps.text: Keep reviewing clinic leaflets with receptionists and quote those hours
Continue usual monthly transfer into four-month reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the designers that a machine may write and arrange routine leaflets, but the agency must show what happens to paid review time. I would ask colleagues to sign a joint request for the new staffing plan and the error-correction budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the owner may keep me for difficult public briefs but cut a junior designer's week first. If the work later narrows to one lead and a screen, my own hours could fall too; four months saved cannot carry that forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would join the team request for written paid review hours and test the agency's new AI language-checker on ten older clinic notices during paid time if the owner approves it. In the first year routine layouts move, I would keep handling public proofs and compare my actual weekly hours with the staffing plan; if my hours fall, I would inspect posted design-production jobs with written wages and hours covering rent after the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly because I can see the junior week being cut before anyone calls it redundancy. A signed notice on a wall is worth more than a perfectly generated one nobody can follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new checker need to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One old leaflet sent people to the wrong clinic entrance. I would log whether the checker notices the missing map cue, not just whether it rewrites the sentence neatly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a production job on its title alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would check the bus timetable as well as written full-week pay and hours; the job has to cover rent after fare and start after a bus I can catch.

I would say **routine leaflet layouts** may move to software.
think: I expect **junior hours** to be cut first, with my own week also at risk.
I cannot live indefinitely on a **four-month reserve** if one lead replaces the team.
do: Join the team request for **staffing and review hours**.
Test the new **AI language-checker** on ten clinic notices on paid time if approved.

feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller team and possible loss of my own hours.

fieldNote: His **group request** concerns staffing and the paid correction work junior designers perform.

steps.text: Join designers’ joint request for written staffing plan and paid correction hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio full AGI by 2028 could make whole campaigns before we finish a brief; the later robots around 2031 do not save screen design. I would ask the four of us to demand written closure dates and any paid correction duties together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our campaign fees to go, and my own job could end even though I know the tools. Four months saved buys a search, not years of rent, and the other agencies may lose the same public clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would make a plain list of the agency's paid briefs and join the team's request for written change dates. If my paid design job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid signage-production or public-information jobs; I would keep offered agency work and accept a new role only on written full-week wages and hours covering rent after travel, with a safe bus start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the team and my own wage. Four months of savings is a calendar, not another employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you already know how to operate sign-cutting equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know how to prepare readable art, not how to run a cutter safely, and I would ask a shop to show me the paid duties before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training for a sign shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid vacancy actually requires it and the shop funds the course and pays the training hours. I will not spend the rent buffer learning a machine for a job that is not open.

say: I would say **2028 AGI** threatens whole campaigns before later robots arrive.
I would join colleagues seeking **written change dates** and paid correction duties.
think: I expect **campaign fees** and possibly my own job to disappear.
I see **four months saved** as search time, while other agencies may lose clients too.
do: List **paid briefs** and join the team request for written change dates now.
Inspect **paid sign-shop duties** before applying after job loss for posted paid signage or public-information roles; keep offered agency hours.
Accept only **weekly wages and hours** covering rent after travel with a usable bus start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely team losses and possible loss of my own wage.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is a calendar, not another employer.
fieldNote: Daily AI skill cannot preserve **campaign fees** if clients purchase full AGI output.
He would take required **sign-equipment training** only for a posted paid vacancy with funded course and paid hours.

steps.text: Join designers asking together for written closure dates and paid correction duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the studio time to argue for paid work that checks public information, not merely a nicer image. Robots reach hands-on work around 2034, so I would be careful about promising a lifetime in sign production.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how signs survive rain, glare and poor lighting while the agency still pays me. I still think 2031 AGI will shrink screen-design fees, and a physical sign is not a guaranteed escape after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask a local sign maker for one paid observation day and bring a clinic wayfinding design to test in the workshop. If offered, I would learn mounting and material checks beside a trained worker; in the first year after 2031, if my agency hours fall, I would apply for an advertised paid production role only if its written weekly wages and hours cover rent after travel and the bus works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to test something real. A glossy screen mock-up cannot show whether a patient sees a sign in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the observation day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hold the sample at the actual clinic entrance and record where the arrow disappears in glare. I would not touch cutting equipment without a worker teaching the safety rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does an observed sign solve the wage question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. One paid day is evidence about the work, not a full week of income; I would need a posted opening with written wages and hours before changing jobs.

say: I would argue for **paid public-information checks** during the five-year warning.
I would note **2034 robots** could later affect physical production.
think: I could learn **materials and mounting** while agency wages continue.
I expect **2031 AGI** to shrink design fees; signs are no permanent shelter.
do: Ask for a **paid sign-shop observation day** and test clinic wayfinding in real light.
Learn **mounting checks** on an offered paid day; avoid cutting equipment without trained-worker safety instruction.
After 2031 hour cuts, apply for **advertised paid production** on written rent-covering weekly wages and hours after travel and usable bus.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though a paid test could show whether sign work fits.
S3.quote: A glossy screen mock-up cannot show whether a patient sees a sign in the rain.
fieldNote: He tests **physical visibility** and safety at a real entrance, not a speculative job label.
An observation day is **not weekly income**; his move requires a posted role, pay, hours and bus access.

steps.text: Ask sign maker for offered paid observation day and test clinic wayfinding
Learn mounting checks on paid day; avoid cutters until trained worker teaches safety rules
Keep agency wages while testing physical sign work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends a decade is long enough to measure public access, not just decorate a page. I would push for agencies and local authorities to publish how many people can actually follow a notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be doing different work by 2036, but I would like to keep earning from real access checks rather than sell a prediction about safe design. Four months saved is useful now; it does not prove a future wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep my agency job and ask the local clinic whether it will pay for a small on-site notice test, with a written fee before I book helpers. If the agency agrees this is outside its client work and the clinic books it, I would pay the helpers, record travel costs and save only the remainder. Each year I would compare paid access-check bookings with my wage; in the first year after 2036, if design hours fall, I would take only a posted paid public-service role whose written full-week wages and hours cover rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant job market, but I can test a small service without pretending to own a consultancy. A signed fee for a real access check would teach me more than ten years of slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help with that clinic test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two people who use the clinic to read the notice from the actual bus stop and pay them for the time. I would not use a volunteer crowd to make a paid report for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the agency if the first test sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A single clinic fee is not a salary, and I would ask the agency for permission first because it has public-health clients.

I would say **real readers** matter more than decorative design.
think: I want **paid access checks**, not predictions about future design safety.
I know **four months saved** cannot guarantee my 2036 wage.
do: Keep agency work; seek its **client-conflict permission** before offering clinic access testing.
Secure a **written clinic fee** before booking helpers; if work proceeds, pay readers, deduct travel and save only remainder.
Compare bookings with wages yearly; after 2036 hour cuts, take only **posted paid public-service work** on written after-travel rent-covering full-week terms.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the distant market but able to test a modest service.
S4.quote: A single clinic fee is not a salary, and I would ask the agency for permission first because it has public-health clients.
fieldNote: His political instinct becomes a **measurable access test** with paid participants, not unpaid goodwill.
Agency permission, a **written clinic fee** and net proceeds protect him from treating a trial as a wage.

steps.text: Keep agency job and obtain agency permission before approaching clinic
Secure written clinic fee before booking two paid readers; deduct travel from proceeds
Save remaining paid clinic-test proceeds after reader and travel costs
After 2036 hour cuts, take posted paid work; written weekly wages/hours cover rent after travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture, because a four-month reserve cannot carry the whole studio if fees vanish. Written dates, paid correction work and an actual posted opening with usable hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to read the public notice before it goes up. If nobody budgets for the reader, the clinic wall becomes a very polished mistake.

headlineQuote: If nobody budgets for the reader, the clinic wall becomes a very polished mistake.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old lead designer** with a master’s degree and strong public-information skills at a small agency.
He earns **typical design pay**, rents alone and holds four months of savings.
He uses AI **daily** for early layouts but measures whether clinic readers understand the final notice.
As AGI arrives sooner, he joins **group staffing requests**, tests paid sign work and explores paid access checks.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could erase studio fees and his wage before he finds a usable paid opening.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written change dates** and paid correction duties for the team.
A **posted role** needs rent-covering wages, hours and a usable bus; required training needs funded fees and paid time.
